main.title: Metal Warriors
main.subtitle: LucasArts · Super Nintendo Entertainment System
main.summary: Metal Warriors is LucasArts' Super Nintendo action game about Lieutenant Stone piloting combat suits against the Dark Axis. The side-scrolling missions combine shooting with exploration, and several different machines can be used during the same operation. The pilot can leave one suit and search for another, turning a robot into a piece of equipment rather than a permanent identity. A vehicle that initially looks like the player's character becomes one possible answer to the terrain and enemies waiting in the next part of the mission.

cards.heading: The pilot can leave the machine
cards.text: Metal Warriors is LucasArts' Super Nintendo action game about Lieutenant Stone piloting combat suits against the Dark Axis. The side-scrolling missions combine shooting with exploration, and several different machines can be used during the same operation. The pilot can leave one suit and search for another, turning a robot into a piece of equipment rather than a permanent identity. A vehicle that initially looks like the player's character becomes one possible answer to the terrain and enemies waiting in the next part of the mission.

cards.heading: Find the suit that fits the problem
cards.text: Six suit types have different weapons and movement characteristics. An agile machine, a heavily armed walker and a specialised climbing unit give the same environment different possibilities. Power-ups can add weapons and restore damage, while taking enough punishment can disable useful equipment. The choice of machine affects how a route can be crossed as much as how an enemy is attacked. Leaving a damaged suit creates a vulnerable interval for the pilot, making the search for a replacement part of the mission's tension.

cards.heading: A shared engine, another scale of action
cards.text: Designers Mike Ebert and Dean Sharpe brought experience from Zombies Ate My Neighbors, with the project using an improved version of that game's engine. Konami published Metal Warriors in North America in 1995. A two-player competitive mode lets the machines and their differences meet directly outside the campaign. Its defining idea remains the relationship between pilot and suit: a formidable body can be abandoned, taken over or replaced, so recognising the next useful machine is as important as firing the weapon already in hand.

main.title: Knuckles' Chaotix
main.subtitle: Two characters joined by a ring
main.summary: Knuckles' Chaotix is Sega's platform game, first released for 32X in Japan on 21 April 1995.

cards.heading: Two characters joined by a ring
cards.text: Knuckles' Chaotix is Sega's platform game, first released for 32X in Japan on 21 April 1995. Knuckles and a group of allies try to stop Doctor Robotnik and Metal Sonic from exploiting the power of mysterious rings. Its stages retain the series' rings, enemies and bright mechanical landscapes, but movement revolves around two characters connected by an elastic tether. A partner can be controlled by the computer or another player. Their relationship becomes the main tool for crossing the stage, replacing a solitary run with movement that must account for another body.

cards.heading: Movement through a partner
cards.text: The connection behaves like a rubber band, allowing one character's position and momentum to affect the other. Handling it successfully requires judging both figures rather than only the one directly controlled. Their individual abilities add further possibilities: Knuckles glides and climbs, Mighty wall-jumps, Espio moves along walls and ceilings, Vector boosts through the air and Charmy flies. A useful pairing therefore changes how the tether can be employed around the landscape. The stage becomes a space for arranging the two characters before releasing the movement built between them.

cards.heading: A different branch of Sonic
cards.text: The tether idea began in the Mega Drive prototype Sonic Crackers before the project moved to 32X and adopted its final cast. Junko Shiratsu and Mariko Nanba composed the score, accompanying one of the add-on's most distinctive original releases. The unusual physics divided players, while several of its characters later returned elsewhere in the series. Its identity remains tied to that experiment in partnership: familiar platform elements are still present, but even an ordinary jump or burst of speed depends on understanding where the companion is and how the connection will respond.

main.title: Astal
main.subtitle: A world made from a jewel
main.summary: Astal is Sega's side-scrolling platform adventure, first released for Saturn in Japan on 28 April 1995.

cards.heading: A world made from a jewel
cards.text: Astal is Sega's side-scrolling platform adventure, first released for Saturn in Japan on 28 April 1995. Its story takes place on Quartalia, a world created from a jewel, where Astal was made to protect Leda. Their separation sends him across brightly coloured landscapes to find her. Hand-drawn graphics give the world a storybook appearance, supported by animated sequences produced by Tokyo Movie Shinsha. The visual detail makes the setting an important part of the journey, while Astal's strength lets him interact with its objects in unusually direct ways.

cards.heading: Strength in the scenery
cards.text: Astal can strike and throw enemies, punch the ground to stun nearby opponents and charge a powerful breath that blows obstacles away. Trees and rocks can also be lifted and thrown. These actions make the landscape a source of practical tools, with a large object becoming something to use rather than simply pass. Running and jumping still carry him across gaps, but encounters often ask which form of strength fits the situation. A group nearby may be easier to stun with a ground strike than meet one opponent at a time.

cards.heading: A bird beside the journey
cards.text: A bird companion adds another layer to the action. Defeating special glowing enemies fills a meter that allows Astal to call on the bird's help, while a second player can take control of its attacks in an asymmetrical cooperative mode. The two characters therefore contribute in different ways to the same stage. Tatsuyuki Maeda and Tatsuya Kousaki composed the music. Alongside the hand-drawn environments, the companion and Astal's exaggerated physical actions give the adventure the quality of an animated tale whose scenery can be touched, lifted and thrown.

main.title: Jumping Flash!
main.subtitle: A rabbit above the landscape
main.summary: Jumping Flash! is Exact and Ultra's first-person platform game for PlayStation, released in Japan on 28 April 1995. Robbit, a mechanical rabbit, searches Crater Planet for jet pods stolen by Baron Aloha. Instead of watching a character cross the screen, the player looks through Robbit's eyes and launches high above the scenery. The combination makes height the main attraction: platforms become small landing places seen from the sky. Its bright islands and unusual viewpoint offered an early demonstration of how a console platformer could inhabit three dimensions.

cards.heading: A rabbit above the landscape
cards.text: Jumping Flash! is Exact and Ultra's first-person platform game for PlayStation, released in Japan on 28 April 1995. Robbit, a mechanical rabbit, searches Crater Planet for jet pods stolen by Baron Aloha. Instead of watching a character cross the screen, the player looks through Robbit's eyes and launches high above the scenery. The combination makes height the main attraction: platforms become small landing places seen from the sky. Its bright islands and unusual viewpoint offered an early demonstration of how a console platformer could inhabit three dimensions.

cards.heading: Finding the landing
cards.text: Robbit can jump three times before landing. The second and third leaps lift him far above the ground, while the camera tilts downward to show his shadow and the surface below. That movement solves a practical problem of first-person jumping: judging where the character will come down. A radar helps locate jet pods, enemies and items, and a timer keeps exploration moving. Looking around reveals the destination; the leap changes how that same space is understood, turning a distant ledge into a possible route through the stage.

cards.heading: Fireworks in the sky
cards.text: A weak laser gives Robbit a regular attack, while collected fireworks provide stronger answers to enemies. Rockets, cherry bombs and other effects add bursts of colour to the journey. The game reused technology from Exact's earlier X68000 title Geograph Seal, adapting its first-person movement for PlayStation. Reviewers welcomed the graphics and unusual approach to platforming. Jumping Flash! 2 and Robbit Mon Dieu continued the character's adventures, but this first outing remains a particularly direct record of developers learning to make height, aiming and landing readable in a new kind of space.

main.title: Full Throttle
main.subtitle: Ben takes the adventure onto the road
main.summary: Tim Schafer's Full Throttle uses voice acting, animation and motorcycle action to tell a compact LucasArts road adventure.

cards.heading: A biker in a LucasArts adventure
cards.text: Full Throttle is Tim Schafer's LucasArts adventure about Ben, a biker caught in a world of engines and corporations. Voice acting, animation and motorcycle sequences give its compact story the pace of a road movie. In 2025, Double Fine examined surviving records and identified May 19, 1995, as the most plausible release date, while retaining an explicit note of uncertainty.

cards.heading: Recovering a release date
cards.text: Double Fine's investigation found that some commonly listed April release dates conflicted with files modified in May on the game disc. Advertisements, newspapers and online archives supplied further clues. Usenet requests for help appeared on May 19, establishing that players had obtained the game by that day. The surviving evidence supported a probable date without establishing one simultaneous retail launch everywhere.

cards.heading: The voice of Ben
cards.text: Roy Conrad's voice performance, Ben's dry dialogue and his animation establish the biker's character. Short exchanges convey both his outward toughness and his loyalty. The CD-ROM format accommodates recorded speech and music, while pauses and restrained delivery give individual lines room to work. Ben's presence helps hold the futuristic road setting together.

cards.heading: Puzzles and motorcycle action
cards.text: Motorcycle chases, road combat and animated transitions connect the adventure's locations. Puzzles remain central, but they are arranged within a relatively compact story. Music, movement and editing carry scenes forward as Ben travels, giving the journey a rhythm different from simply walking between static adventure-game screens.

main.title: Light Crusader
main.subtitle: Below Green Row
main.summary: Light Crusader is Treasure's action adventure, first released for Mega Drive in Japan on 26 May 1995.

cards.heading: Below Green Row
cards.text: Light Crusader is Treasure's action adventure, first released for Mega Drive in Japan on 26 May 1995. Sir David arrives in Green Row, where inhabitants have been disappearing, and enters the dungeon beneath the town to investigate. Its rooms use an isometric view, giving platforms, movable objects and passages a visible sense of depth. David fights with a sword, but reaching the next chamber often requires understanding how the space works. The town above provides a place to speak to people and buy supplies between expeditions below.

cards.heading: Moving through a puzzle
cards.text: David can run, jump and attack while standing or moving, so the dungeon asks the player to judge position as well as choose a direction. Objects can be moved into useful places, and the arrangement of a room often provides the clues to its solution. Isometric depth makes a gap or ledge less immediately obvious than it would be in a side view. Reaching it successfully comes from connecting the visible layout with David's movement, then carrying out that short sequence while enemies or hazards occupy the same space.

cards.heading: Four elements to combine
cards.text: Magic is organised around fire, water, wind and earth. Combining the elements produces different spells, while water also supplies a way to restore health. The system gives the collected elements a purpose beyond a single fixed attack, inviting experimentation when a room or enemy becomes troublesome. Light Crusader was Treasure's final Mega Drive release, and its construction differs markedly from the studio's faster shooting games. Much of its appeal comes from the small discovery inside a chamber: a useful combination, a movable obstacle or a route that becomes clear once viewed from another angle.

main.title: Street Fighter Alpha
main.summary: Street Fighter Alpha: Warriors' Dreams, known as Street Fighter Zero in Japan, Asia, South America, and Oceania, is a 1995 fighting game developed and published by Capcom for arcades.

cards.heading: Younger warriors enter the tournament
cards.text: Street Fighter Alpha: Warriors' Dreams, known as Street Fighter Zero in Japan, Asia, South America, and Oceania, is a 1995 fighting game developed and published by Capcom for arcades. It was the first all-new Street Fighter game produced by Capcom since 1991's Street Fighter II. Plotwise, it serves as a prequel to Street Fighter II and thus features younger versions of established characters, as well as characters from the original Street Fighter and Final Fight.

cards.heading: Super Combos and a new visual style
cards.text: The game introduces several new features, expanding on the Super Combo system previously featured in Super Street Fighter II Turbo, with graphics drawn in a similar art style to the one Capcom employed in Darkstalkers and X-Men: Children of the Atom. After its arcade release, it was ported to PlayStation and Sega Saturn home consoles. Street Fighter Alpha received a mainly positive reception; it was followed up by Street Fighter Alpha 2 in 1996 as part of the Alpha sub-series.

main.title: Donkey Kong Land
main.subtitle: A new jungle in a pocket
main.summary: Donkey Kong Land brings Rare’s Donkey Kong platforming to Game Boy as a separate adventure, with new stages built for the handheld. Donkey Kong and Diddy pursue the stolen banana hoard through four worlds and thirty levels. The game retains the recognisable character rendering associated with Donkey Kong Country, compressing that look into a small monochrome display. Its challenge lies in making the pair’s movement readable within those limits, while offering a journey that gives owners of the console game something different to discover.

cards.heading: A new jungle in a pocket
cards.text: Donkey Kong Land brings Rare’s Donkey Kong platforming to Game Boy as a separate adventure, with new stages built for the handheld. Donkey Kong and Diddy pursue the stolen banana hoard through four worlds and thirty levels. The game retains the recognisable character rendering associated with Donkey Kong Country, compressing that look into a small monochrome display. Its challenge lies in making the pair’s movement readable within those limits, while offering a journey that gives owners of the console game something different to discover.

cards.heading: Two ways through a stage
cards.text: Donkey Kong and Diddy share the journey but offer different physical qualities: strength and agility change how an encounter feels. Barrels, bananas and hidden bonus areas give the route its familiar rhythm, while animal helpers add variations. The scenery moves beyond jungle territory into places such as clouds and a city, helping establish the handheld game’s own identity. Reaching an exit is one aim; recognising a possible bonus entrance or deciding how to approach an enemy gives the same stretch of level another layer.

cards.heading: A handheld interpretation
cards.text: The Game Boy’s screen could not reproduce the Super Nintendo presentation directly. Donkey Kong Land instead fits its rendered characters and platform structures to a much smaller visual field. Collecting the KONG letters provides access to saving, tying a useful feature to exploration within a stage. These adjustments make the game an example of adaptation through new design. It carries familiar characters, sounds and actions into a different machine, while the level layouts and handheld constraints give the resulting adventure its own shape.

main.title: Clockwork Knight 2
main.subtitle: Another night for Pepper
main.summary: Clockwork Knight 2 is Sega's platform sequel, first released for Saturn in Japan on 28 July 1995.

cards.heading: Another night for Pepper
cards.text: Clockwork Knight 2 is Sega's platform sequel, first released for Saturn in Japan on 28 July 1995. It continues the first game's ending: Chelsea has returned but remains asleep, and another abduction sends Pepper after her again. The toy knight still fights with his key and moves through household environments whose scale makes him vulnerable to ordinary objects. New rooms and more varied stage sequences expand the journey, retaining the mixture of pre-rendered characters and polygonal scenery that gave the original its miniature theatrical appearance.

cards.heading: A reason to search the room
cards.text: Four playing cards are hidden in each main level. Finding all four earns a gold key, while collecting the full set of thirty-two provides a level-selection code. Those rewards give the room's concealed passages a purpose beyond an immediate life or score bonus. Some stages carry Pepper forward automatically, changing the pace of the platforming. Others let him ride his donkey Barobaro, whose detachable head can be launched at enemies. The familiar key attack therefore shares the adventure with new ways to move and clear a path.

cards.heading: A larger box of toys
cards.text: Hidden obstacle races provide additional challenges, while the North American edition includes Bosses Galore, a mode drawn from the Japanese compilation of both games. Pepper or Ginger can face bosses from the two adventures and receive a ranking for their performance. The main journey moves through a child's room, a study, a bathroom and a clock tower, giving the sequel a different set of household objects to transform. Its strongest additions reward returning to those spaces, finding the concealed cards and learning the short sequences that make each room work.

main.title: Gakkō de Atta Kowai Hanashi
main.subtitle: Six students, many unsettling stories
main.summary: On August 4, 1995 Gakkō de Atta Kowai Hanashi arrived on Super Famicom.

cards.heading: Choosing whose story comes next
cards.text: On August 4, 1995 Gakkō de Atta Kowai Hanashi arrived on Super Famicom. Six students tell unsettling stories to a school reporter, but the order in which they are heard and the player's choices alter routes, details and conclusions. The game uses photographs, text and sound to build everyday horror around corridors, clubs and school legends. Fear builds around the suspicion that a familiar story may branch simply because a different person told it in a different way.

cards.heading: Photographs and a small studio
cards.text: The game uses digitised photographs in its in-game graphics. It was developed by Pandora Box, the studio founded by designer and scenario writer Takeo Iijima. Its characters and setting later became part of the Apathy visual- and sound-novel franchise.

cards.heading: More than fifty scenarios
cards.text: In the game you play as a reporter for the school paper, writing a story about the 7 School Mysteries. Each mystery is told to you by one of 6 possible other students. As you make your way through each scenario, you are given choices which will change the outcome of the story and therefore your progression through the game. Including hidden stories, there are more than 50 possible scenarios in the game.

cards.heading: An expanded PlayStation version
cards.text: Gakkou de atta Kowai Hanashi S followed on PlayStation in 1996. It added improved graphics, full-motion video and further narrative paths. This version also lets players choose the gender of the main character.
